## Case and decision {#sec-b04-case}

Six months after the board meeting in @sec-b03, a fictional rehabilitation physician is asked to include one number
in a grant report: mean gait speed 0.56 m/s in weeks three to five after surgery, n = 7 of 12 patients. She asks the
physiotherapy team to regenerate it. They find a spreadsheet called `final_v3_corrected.xlsx`, a figure pasted into a
slide and no script. A colleague remembers that the sensor-mat values were “divided by 100 somewhere”, that one
patient identifier was fixed by hand and that a duplicate row was deleted. Nobody can say in which order, or whether
anything else happened. The physician has to decide whether the number may go into the report. The department
decides on a rule for the future: a number leaves the team only if one command can regenerate it from the raw exports.

## Core reading {#sec-b04-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended for W1, W6 and W8 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

### Reproducible is a modest, checkable promise

A result is *reproducible* when the same data and the same code produce the same number. This is less than
*replication*, which asks whether new data lead to the same conclusion. Peng described reproducibility as the
minimum standard for judging a computational claim when full replication is not possible [@peng2011reproducible].
It is modest because it says nothing about whether the analysis is right. It is valuable because anyone can check it,
and because every error that is found can be traced to a line of code.

The spreadsheet in the case fails this standard not because spreadsheets are bad, but because the steps that changed
the data were performed by hand and left no trace. Such *hidden interactive steps* are common: editing cells,
filtering in a viewer and copying the visible rows, retyping a number from one window into another. Some are not even
chosen by the user. Ziemann and colleagues found that about one-fifth of genomics papers with supplementary Excel
gene lists contained gene names that the software had silently converted into dates or numbers (*published*)
[@ziemann2016genenames].

Sandve and colleagues condensed the remedy into ten rules [@sandve2013tenrules]. Five of them carry this chapter:
keep track of how every result was produced; avoid manual data manipulation; archive the exact versions of the
software used; put all custom scripts under version control; and, for analyses with randomness, record the seed.

### A project that runs with one command

Wilson and colleagues describe “good enough” practices for researchers without formal training in programming
[@wilson2017goodenough]. Applied to the fracture cohort, they lead to a small folder structure:

```text
hip-gait-project/
├── README.md               start instructions, data schema, target value
├── ARTEFACTS.csv           provenance, rights and data status of every exported file
├── run.R                   the one command:  Rscript run.R
├── R/                      code, numbered in the order it runs
│   ├── 00_visits.R         planned-visit table of chapter B03 (synthetic)
│   ├── 01_simulate_raw.R   raw exports (in a real project: delivered, read-only)
│   ├── 02_clean.R          documented cleaning instead of manual edits
│   ├── 03_check.R          counts on two independent paths
│   └── 04_figure.R         figure and target value
├── data/raw/               written once, never edited
├── data/derived/           always regenerated, never edited by hand
├── output/                 figure, session information
└── report/report.qmd       Quarto report: text and numbers from the same code
```

Three conventions do most of the work. First, *raw data are read-only*; every change happens in code. Second, every
path is *relative* to the project folder, such as `data/raw/sensormat.csv`, never `C:/Users/anna/Desktop/...`, so the
folder runs on any computer. Third, the project states a **target value**, a number that must come out, and stops
with an error if it does not. Here it is the number from the case: in visit window V4, 7 of 12 patients measured, mean
gait speed 0.56 m/s.

### What a colleague needs to rerun it

A colleague who receives the folder should not need to ask anything. The README answers four questions in this
order: how to start (one command), what the input files contain (the *data schema*: one line per file with its unit
of observation, its key and the unit of every measured column), which number must come out (the target value), and
under which terms the files may be used. The data schema is where the case went wrong: the stopwatch export gives
seconds for four metres, the sensor mat gives centimetres per second, and only the conversion written in code makes
both comparable. The second safeguard is the count on two paths, as in @sec-b03. Patients, measurements and linked records are
computed once from the visit table and once from the patient table with different functions; any lost or duplicated
row shows up as a disagreement. Both checks are cheap, and both fail loudly instead of producing a plausible figure.

### Versions of code, data and software

A project changes over time. **Git**, a version control system, records every change to text files with author, date
and a short message, so that the state of the code on the day a figure was made can be restored [@bryan2018versioncontrol].
The R function `sessionInfo()` records the versions of R and of every loaded package; it belongs in every report.
**Quarto** turns a text file with embedded R code into a report in which every number in the text is computed, not
typed [@quarto-books]. Text and figure can then no longer drift apart.

### Every exported file carries its passport

Files travel: into slides, e-mails, other projects. Once they leave the project folder, they lose their context.
Each exported artefact therefore needs three pieces of information that travel with it: its *provenance* (which code
made it from which input), its *rights* (who may use it under which licence) and its *data status* (synthetic,
published, real and pseudonymised, aggregate). @tbl-b04-artefacts shows them for the project in this chapter.

| Artefact | Produced by | Provenance | Rights | Data status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `data/raw/*.csv` (4 files) | `R/01_simulate_raw.R` | Generated from the planned-visit table of @sec-b03 | CC BY 4.0 | *synthetic* |
| `data/derived/visits.csv` | `R/02_clean.R` | From the four raw files; cleaning log: 1 duplicate removed, 1 identifier corrected | CC BY 4.0 | *synthetic* |
| `output/figure-windows.png` | `R/04_figure.R` | From `data/derived/visits.csv` | CC BY 4.0 | *synthetic*, aggregate |
| `output/session-info.txt` | `run.R` | Software versions of the run | CC BY 4.0 | technical metadata |
| `report/report.html` | Quarto, `report/report.qmd` | Text, figure and numbers from the files above | Text CC BY 4.0; code MIT | *synthetic*, aggregate |
| `R/*.R`, `run.R` | Authors | — | MIT | code, no data |

: Provenance, rights and data status of every exported artefact of the teaching project (n = 12 *synthetic* patients). In a project with real data, the rights column would name the data use agreement and ethics approval, and the raw files would not be released. {#tbl-b04-artefacts}

**A number counts as reproduced only if code alone regenerates it from the raw exports in a fresh R session and it
matches the stated target value. A number that is retyped or copied counts as unreproduced, however plausible it
looks.**

**Question for the workshop:** Give your script and raw files to another group. They start a fresh R session, run
one command and report the target value. Which file, package or step did they need that was not in your project?

## Lab {#sec-b04-lab}

### Step 1: R objects in five minutes

R works with *objects* that have a name. The most important are *vectors* (a sequence of values of one type) and
*data frames* (several vectors of equal length side by side). Ms K.'s five gait-speed values from @sec-b03 serve as
example.

```{r}
#| label: b04-objects
gait <- c(0.31, 0.42, 0.55, 0.63, 0.78)    # numeric vector, metres per second
day  <- c(2, 6, 15, 27, 91)                 # days since surgery
length(gait)                                # how many values
mean(gait)                                  # one number from five
gait[day > 10]                              # values after day 10: logical selection with [ ]
class(gait)                                 # the type of the object

with_gap <- c(0.31, NA, 0.55)               # NA = not available
mean(with_gap)                              # NA is contagious ...
mean(with_gap, na.rm = TRUE)                # ... unless it is removed on purpose
```

The last two lines are the whole of @sec-b03 in miniature: R refuses to average over a missing value until you tell it
to, and from then on the denominator is smaller without anyone seeing it.

### Step 2: reading a file with a relative path

The planned-visit table was saved by @sec-b03 in the book's `data` folder. This chapter lives in the `chapters`
folder, so the relative path goes one level up (`..`) and then into `data`.

```{r}
#| label: b04-read
path_b03 <- file.path("..", "data", "b03-visits.csv")
stopifnot(file.exists(path_b03))
visits_b03 <- read.csv(path_b03, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
str(visits_b03)
```

`str()` shows the *structure*: 60 rows (observations), 6 columns (variables), the type of each column (`chr` for
text, `int` or `num` for numbers) and the first values. Missing values appear as `NA`. If R reports “cannot open
file”, the working directory is not the folder you think; `getwd()` shows where R is looking.

### Step 3: a base graphic

Base R draws graphics without additional packages. `cdsr_par()` sets the book's margins and fonts; `plot()` draws
points and lines; `text()` writes labels at given coordinates. The function below is the figure of the project, and
it is used again in Step 7.

```{r}
#| label: b04-figure-functions
summarise_windows <- function(visits) {
  data.frame(window  = sort(unique(visits$window)),
             n       = as.vector(tapply(visits$status == "measured", visits$window, sum)),
             of      = as.vector(table(visits$window)),
             mean_ms = as.vector(tapply(visits$gait_ms, visits$window, mean, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
draw_windows <- function(s) {
  plot(seq_len(nrow(s)), s$mean_ms, type = "b", pch = 16, ylim = c(0, 1), xlim = c(0.5, nrow(s) + 0.5), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Planned visit window", ylab = "Mean gait speed (m/s)")
  axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(s)), labels = s$window)
  text(seq_len(nrow(s)), s$mean_ms, paste0("n = ", s$n, "/", s$of), pos = 3, cex = 0.85)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-windows
#| fig-cap: "Mean gait speed (m/s) of the patients measured in each planned visit window (V1 days 1–3 to V5 days 80–100 after surgery), with the observed denominator above each point. Base R graphic. n = 12 patients; *synthetic*."
#| fig-alt: "Base R line chart with five points for visit windows V1 to V5, rising from about 0.33 to 0.75 metres per second. Above the points the labels read n = 9/12, 11/12, 8/12, 7/12 and 7/12."
#| fig-height: 4
cdsr_par()
draw_windows(summarise_windows(visits_b03))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="What you should see"}
Five points joined by lines, rising from left to right; the vertical axis runs from 0 to 1 m/s. The labels above the
points read `n = 9/12`, `n = 11/12`, `n = 8/12`, `n = 7/12` and `n = 7/12`. The fourth point, V4, lies just above
0.55 m/s: this is the target value of the project.
:::

### Step 4: long and wide

The table has one row per planned visit: the *long* format. Many spreadsheets use the *wide* format instead, with one
row per patient and one column per visit. Base R's `reshape()` converts between the two.

```{r}
#| label: b04-reshape
wide <- reshape(visits_b03[, c("pid", "window", "gait_ms")],
                idvar = "pid", timevar = "window", direction = "wide")
head(wide, 4)
long_again <- reshape(wide, direction = "long")
stopifnot(dim(wide) == c(12, 6), nrow(long_again) == 60,
          sum(!is.na(wide[, -1])) == 42)      # still 42 measured values
```

The wide table looks tidier on screen but has lost two things: the actual day of each visit and the reason for each
missing value. In the wide table, `NA` for patient `P04` in V3 (at home) and `NA` for `P05` in V3 (died) look
identical. Wickham's definition of *tidy data* — each variable a column, each observation a row, each type of
observational unit a table — is the reason why the project keeps the long format and a separate patient table
[@wickham2014tidy].

### Step 5: start instructions and data schema

The README is the first file a colleague opens. It needs only four parts.

```text
# hip-gait-project (synthetic teaching data)

## Start
1. Install R (version used: see output/session-info.txt) and Quarto.
2. Open a terminal in this folder and run:   Rscript run.R
3. Expected: "Done. Target value V4: 0.56 m/s (n = 7 of 12)". Any other result stops with an error.

## Data schema (data/raw/, read-only)
patients.csv   one row per patient     pid, age (years), sex, fracture, end_day (days since surgery), end_reason
visit_log.csv  one row per planned visit  pid, window (V1-V5), day (days since surgery), status
stopwatch.csv  one row per ward/outpatient test  pid, day, time_4m_s (seconds for 4 metres)
sensormat.csv  one row per rehabilitation test   pid, day, speed_cm_s (centimetres per second)
Key: pid (patients) = pid (all other files); pid + day identifies a test.

## Target value
Visit window V4: 7 of 12 patients measured, mean gait speed 0.564 m/s (rounded 0.56).

## Rights and data status
Synthetic data, CC BY 4.0. Code under MIT licence. See ARTEFACTS.csv.
```

The schema states the unit of every measurement column, and the units differ: seconds for 4 metres on the ward, centimetres
per second on the sensor mat. The former manual division by 100 lived exactly here.

### Step 6: the scripts

Each script defines one or two *functions*: named recipes that take an input and return an output. The first one is
the planned-visit table of @sec-b03, copied unchanged; Step 7 checks that it really is unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: b04-script-00
# R/00_visits.R -- planned-visit table of chapter B03 (synthetic); one row = one planned visit
build_visits <- function() {
  windows <- c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4", "V5")
  visit_rows <- function(pid, day, gait_ms, status) {
    data.frame(pid = pid, window = windows, day = day, gait_ms = gait_ms, status = status)
  }
  m <- "measured"
  visits <- rbind(
    visit_rows("P01", c(2, 6, 15, 27, 91), c(.31, .42, .55, .63, .78), rep(m, 5)),
    visit_rows("P02", c(1, 5, 13, 29, 88), c(.28, .35, .47, .58, .70), rep(m, 5)),
    visit_rows("P03", c(2, 6, 14, NA, NA), c(NA, .31, .38, NA, NA),
               c("unable", m, m, "transferred", "transferred")),
    visit_rows("P04", c(3, 8, NA, NA, 90), c(.40, .52, NA, NA, .85),
               c(m, m, "at home", "at home", m)),
    visit_rows("P05", c(1, 4, NA, NA, NA), c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
               c("unable", "unable", "died", "died", "died")),
    visit_rows("P06", c(2, 7, 16, 30, NA), c(.33, .41, .50, .57, NA),
               c(m, m, m, m, "visit missed")),
    visit_rows("P07", c(2, 6, 12, 26, 93), c(.36, .47, .58, .66, .81), rep(m, 5)),
    visit_rows("P08", c(3, 8, 17, 31, NA), c(NA, .30, .29, NA, NA),
               c("unable", m, m, "unable", "transferred")),
    visit_rows("P09", c(2, 5, NA, NA, 90), c(.38, .49, NA, NA, .88),
               c(m, m, "at home", "at home", m)),
    visit_rows("P10", c(2, 9, 18, 28, 90), c(.27, .33, .41, .46, .52), rep(m, 5)),
    visit_rows("P11", c(1, 6, 15, 24, NA), c(.30, .37, .45, .44, NA), c(m, m, m, m, "died")),
    visit_rows("P12", c(3, 7, 14, 28, 89), c(.35, .44, NA, .61, .74),
               c(m, m, "device fault", m, m))
  )
  visits$method <- ifelse(visits$window %in% c("V3", "V4"), "sensor mat", "stopwatch")
  visits$method[is.na(visits$day)] <- NA
  visits
}
```

The second script turns this table into the files the devices and the clinic would deliver: a patient list, a visit
log, a stopwatch export in seconds and a sensor-mat export in centimetres per second, including one duplicated row and
one mistyped identifier, as in the case.

```{r}
#| label: b04-script-01
# R/01_simulate_raw.R -- raw exports (synthetic). In a real project: delivered files, read-only.
simulate_raw <- function() {
  patients <- data.frame(
    pid = sprintf("P%02d", 1:12),
    age = c(84, 79, 91, 76, 93, 82, 80, 88, 74, 86, 90, 78),
    sex = c("f", "f", "f", "m", "f", "f", "m", "f", "f", "m", "f", "f"),
    fracture = c("neck", "pertroch", "pertroch", "neck", "pertroch", "neck",
                 "neck", "pertroch", "neck", "pertroch", "neck", "neck"),
    end_day = c(91, 88, 20, 90, 11, 90, 93, 33, 90, 90, 52, 89),
    end_reason = c("follow-up complete", "follow-up complete", "transferred to nursing home",
                   "follow-up complete", "died", "day-90 visit missed", "follow-up complete",
                   "transferred to acute hospital", "follow-up complete", "follow-up complete",
                   "died", "follow-up complete"))
  visits <- build_visits()
  m <- visits[visits$status == "measured", ]
  ward <- m[m$method == "stopwatch", ]
  stopwatch <- data.frame(pid = ward$pid, day = ward$day,
                          time_4m_s = round(4 / ward$gait_ms, 2))        # seconds for 4 metres
  rehab <- m[m$method == "sensor mat", ]
  sensormat <- data.frame(pid = rehab$pid, day = rehab$day,
                          speed_cm_s = round(100 * rehab$gait_ms))       # centimetres per second
  sensormat <- rbind(sensormat, sensormat[sensormat$pid == "P02" & sensormat$day == 13, ])  # duplicate
  sensormat$pid[sensormat$pid == "P07" & sensormat$day == 12] <- "P7"                        # typing error
  list(patients = patients, visit_log = visits[, c("pid", "window", "day", "status")],
       stopwatch = stopwatch, sensormat = sensormat)
}
```

The third script replaces the hidden spreadsheet step. Every change is written down, and the function stops if the
result is implausible or if a value cannot be linked to exactly one planned visit.

```{r}
#| label: b04-script-02
# R/02_clean.R -- documented cleaning instead of manual edits
id_corrections <- c(P7 = "P07")    # known typing error at the sensor mat, confirmed against the visit log

clean_visits <- function(raw) {
  sw <- raw$stopwatch
  sw$gait_ms <- round(4 / sw$time_4m_s, 2)            # 4 metres / seconds = metres per second
  sm <- raw$sensormat
  n_dup <- sum(duplicated(sm))
  sm <- sm[!duplicated(sm), ]                          # remove exact duplicate exports
  fix <- sm$pid %in% names(id_corrections)
  sm$pid[fix] <- id_corrections[sm$pid[fix]]           # correct known identifier errors
  sm$gait_ms <- sm$speed_cm_s / 100                    # centimetres per second -> metres per second
  values <- rbind(sw[c("pid", "day", "gait_ms")], sm[c("pid", "day", "gait_ms")])
  v <- raw$visit_log
  measured <- v$status == "measured"
  key_visit <- paste(v$pid, v$day)
  key_value <- paste(values$pid, values$day)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(key_value),                 # one value per patient and day
            all(key_value %in% key_visit[measured]),   # every value belongs to a measured visit
            all(key_visit[measured] %in% key_value))   # every measured visit has a value
  v$gait_ms <- ifelse(measured, values$gait_ms[match(key_visit, key_value)], NA)
  stopifnot(all(v$gait_ms[measured] > 0.05 & v$gait_ms[measured] < 2.5))   # plausible range in m/s
  v$method <- ifelse(v$window %in% c("V3", "V4"), "sensor mat", "stopwatch")
  v$method[is.na(v$day)] <- NA
  v <- v[, c("pid", "window", "day", "gait_ms", "status", "method")]
  attr(v, "cleaning_log") <- c(duplicates_removed = n_dup, ids_corrected = sum(fix))
  v
}
```

The fourth script counts patients, measurements and linked records on two independent paths and stops if they
disagree. The fifth script is the pair of figure functions from Step 3.

```{r}
#| label: b04-script-03
# R/03_check.R -- counts on two independent paths
check_counts <- function(visits, patients) {
  a <- c(patients     = length(unique(visits$pid)),                     # path A: visit table
         measurements = sum(visits$status == "measured"),
         linked       = sum(visits$pid[!is.na(visits$gait_ms)] %in% patients$pid))
  per_patient <- tapply(!is.na(visits$gait_ms), visits$pid, sum)       # path B: other objects
  b <- c(patients     = nrow(patients),
         measurements = sum(per_patient),
         linked       = nrow(merge(visits[!is.na(visits$gait_ms), ], patients, by = "pid")))
  stopifnot(identical(a, b), b[["patients"]] == 12, b[["measurements"]] == 42, b[["linked"]] == 42)
  b
}
```

### Step 7: the one command, run inside this chapter

`run.R` calls the scripts in order and writes the files. Because a book chapter must not write project folders, the
same sequence runs here in memory; the listing shows the file version.

```{r}
#| label: b04-run-listing
#| eval: false
# run.R -- one command, run from the project folder:  Rscript run.R
for (f in sort(list.files("R", pattern = "[.]R$", full.names = TRUE))) source(f)
dir.create(file.path("data", "raw"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(file.path("data", "derived"), showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)

raw <- simulate_raw()
for (nm in names(raw)) write.csv(raw[[nm]], file.path("data", "raw", paste0(nm, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
raw_in <- lapply(setNames(names(raw), names(raw)), function(nm)
  read.csv(file.path("data", "raw", paste0(nm, ".csv")), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))

visits <- clean_visits(raw_in)
write.csv(visits, file.path("data", "derived", "visits.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
counts <- check_counts(visits, raw_in$patients)
s <- summarise_windows(visits)
stopifnot(s$n[s$window == "V4"] == 7, abs(s$mean_ms[s$window == "V4"] - 0.564) < 0.001)   # target value

png(file.path("output", "figure-windows.png"), width = 1400, height = 900, res = 200)
draw_windows(s)
invisible(dev.off())
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path("output", "session-info.txt"))
stopifnot(system2("quarto", c("render", file.path("report", "report.qmd"))) == 0)
cat("Done. Target value V4:", round(s$mean_ms[s$window == "V4"], 2), "m/s (n = 7 of 12)\n")
```

In memory, the CSV round trip is simulated with a *text connection*, so that the cleaning step sees exactly what it
would read from disk.

```{r}
#| label: b04-run
as_csv_text <- function(df) capture.output(write.csv(df, row.names = FALSE))
from_csv_text <- function(lines) read.csv(text = lines, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

raw <- simulate_raw()
raw_in <- lapply(raw, function(df) from_csv_text(as_csv_text(df)))
c(device_rows = nrow(raw_in$stopwatch) + nrow(raw_in$sensormat),
  unknown_ids = length(setdiff(c(raw_in$stopwatch$pid, raw_in$sensormat$pid), raw_in$patients$pid)))
setdiff(raw_in$sensormat$pid, raw_in$patients$pid)    # which identifier cannot be linked

visits_new <- clean_visits(raw_in)
attr(visits_new, "cleaning_log")
counts <- check_counts(visits_new, raw_in$patients)
counts
s <- summarise_windows(visits_new)
v4 <- s[s$window == "V4", ]
stopifnot(v4$n == 7, v4$of == 12, abs(v4$mean_ms - 0.564) < 0.001)    # target value
```

The raw exports contain 43 device rows, one of them with an identifier (`P7`) that does not exist in the patient
list. After cleaning, the log reports one duplicate removed and one identifier corrected; the counts agree on both
paths (12 patients, 42 measurements, 42 linked records), and the target value holds: in V4, `r v4$n` of `r v4$of`
patients, mean `r sprintf("%.2f", v4$mean_ms)` m/s.

The last check compares the result with the file that @sec-b03 wrote, cell by cell and as a cryptographic checksum
(SHA-256, computed with the **digest** package). If a single character differed, the checksums would differ.

```{r}
#| label: b04-compare
library(digest)
new_csv <- as_csv_text(visits_new)
b03_csv <- readLines(path_b03)
checksums <- c(rebuilt = digest(paste(new_csv, collapse = "\n"), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE),
               b03_file = digest(paste(b03_csv, collapse = "\n"), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE))
substr(checksums, 1, 16)                                   # first 16 of 64 hexadecimal characters
stopifnot(identical(from_csv_text(new_csv), visits_b03),   # same table, cell by cell
          checksums[["rebuilt"]] == checksums[["b03_file"]])
```

The table rebuilt from raw exports is identical to the one in @sec-b03. The number in the grant report can now be
regenerated by anyone with the project folder.

### Step 8: software version and report

`sessionInfo()` lists the R version, the operating system and the attached packages. Its output belongs at the end of
every report.

```{r}
#| label: b04-session
print(sessionInfo(), locale = FALSE)
```

The Quarto report computes every number it mentions. The `r` inside back-ticks in the text below is evaluated when the
report is rendered.

````markdown
---
title: "Gait speed after hip fracture surgery (synthetic teaching data)"
format: html
---

```{{r}}
#| include: false
source("../R/04_figure.R")
visits <- read.csv("../data/derived/visits.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s <- summarise_windows(visits)
v4 <- s[s$window == "V4", ]
```

In visit window V4 (days 21–35), `r knitr::inline_expr("v4$n")` of `r knitr::inline_expr("v4$of")` patients were measured.
Their mean gait speed was `r knitr::inline_expr('sprintf("%.2f", v4$mean_ms)')` m/s (@fig-windows).

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-windows
#| fig-cap: "Mean gait speed per visit window; n = patients measured of 12 (synthetic)."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of mean gait speed in five visit windows with the number of measured patients above each point."
draw_windows(s)
```

```{{r}}
sessionInfo()
````

### Step 9: version control with Git

Git is run in a terminal, not in R. The commands below put the project under version control; the file `.gitignore`
lists what Git should never record. Derived files are excluded because `run.R` regenerates them. In a project with
real patient data, the raw data folder belongs in `.gitignore` too: a file that was committed once remains in the
history even after it is deleted.

```bash
git init                                   # start recording in this folder
git add README.md run.R R/ report/report.qmd .gitignore
git commit -m "Rebuild gait figure from raw exports; target value V4 = 0.56 m/s"
git log --oneline                          # list of recorded versions
```

```text
# .gitignore
data/derived/
output/
report/report.html
report/report_files/
```

### Step 10: the artefact register

The passport of @tbl-b04-artefacts can itself be produced by code, with a checksum for each data file so that a later
reader can verify that the file in hand is the file described.

```{r}
#| label: b04-artefacts
sha <- function(lines) substr(digest(paste(lines, collapse = "\n"), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE), 1, 12)
artefacts <- data.frame(
  artefact    = c(paste0("data/raw/", names(raw_in), ".csv"), "data/derived/visits.csv"),
  produced_by = c(rep("R/01_simulate_raw.R", 4), "R/02_clean.R"),
  rights      = "CC BY 4.0",
  data_status = "synthetic",
  rows        = c(sapply(raw_in, nrow), nrow(visits_new)),
  sha256_start = c(sapply(raw, function(df) sha(as_csv_text(df))), sha(new_csv))
)
artefacts
stopifnot(artefacts$rows == c(12, 60, 27, 16, 60))
```

The register shows 12 patients, 60 planned visits, 27 stopwatch rows and 16 sensor-mat rows (15 tests plus the
duplicate). Saved as `ARTEFACTS.csv` next to the README, it answers the three questions of the passport for every
data file.

## Counter-check {#sec-b04-countercheck}

A firmware update of the sensor mat changes its export from centimetres per second to metres per second, without
notice. The project is run again unchanged. **Predict first:** does the run finish with a wrong target value, finish
with the right one, or stop — and at which line?

```{r}
#| label: b04-countercheck
raw_updated <- raw_in
raw_updated$sensormat$speed_cm_s <- raw_updated$sensormat$speed_cm_s / 100   # now really m/s
outcome <- tryCatch({
  clean_visits(raw_updated)
  "run finished"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
outcome
stopifnot(outcome != "run finished")
```

The run stops inside `clean_visits()` at the plausibility check: after the now superfluous division by 100,
rehabilitation values of about 0.005 m/s fall outside the range of 0.05 to 2.5 m/s. Without that line, the target
value check would have caught the error one step later, because the V4 mean would have collapsed. In the spreadsheet
version of the project, the same firmware update would have produced a plausible-looking figure with nonsense in two
of its five points. A check that can fail is what turns a script into evidence.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b04-consequences}

**Patients.** An unreproducible number in a grant report or a publication can steer resources and clinical practice.
Patients are not harmed by a missing script directly, but by a decision based on a number nobody can check. The
target value and the two-path count make a silent error visible before it travels.

**Operations.** A department can adopt three simple rules: raw exports are stored read-only; every reported number
comes from a script with a target value; and every exported file has a passport like @tbl-b04-artefacts. Device
changes such as the firmware update need a change log that the analysis team can see.

**Data protection and information security.** Version control, cloud storage and code-sharing platforms are copies.
For real patient data, the rule is: code and documentation may be shared under the conditions agreed, data are not
committed. A raw file that once entered a Git history remains there until the history is rewritten, which is a
security incident to be handled, not a clean-up task (@sec-b24). Pseudonymised identifiers such as `P01` remain
personal data under the GDPR [@eu2016dsgvo]; the key that links them to names is kept apart from the project
(@sec-b23). Which platform an institution permits for which data class is a local decision (*open*, to be clarified
with the data protection officer and IT security).

**Rights.** In this book, text and figures are licensed under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT licence. In a research
project the rights column must name the actual terms: data use agreements, ethics approval, and third-party material
such as device manuals or published figures.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b04-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** Can the number in the main figure be regenerated from the raw data with the published code
  and a single command, and is there a stated target value that the code checks?
- **Self-test:** A colleague sends you `analysis.R`. It starts with `setwd("C:/Users/maria/Documents/thesis")`, loads
  `data_final_clean.csv` and draws the figure. There is no other file. List three things you need before you can say
  whether the figure is reproducible.

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
  (1) The raw data and the code that produced `data_final_clean.csv` from them; “final clean” suggests hidden steps.
  (2) A project folder with relative paths instead of `setwd()` to a personal directory, so that it runs on another
  computer. (3) A target value (the number the figure should show) and the software versions (`sessionInfo()`); with
  random elements also the seed. Useful in addition: a data dictionary with units and the Git history.
  :::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @peng2011reproducible — reproducibility as the minimum standard for computational claims.
  - @sandve2013tenrules — ten rules, five of which structure the project in this chapter.
  - @wilson2017goodenough — practical project organisation for researchers without programming training.
  - @ziemann2016genenames — a *published* example of silent spreadsheet conversions in the literature.
  - @wickham2014tidy — the definition of tidy (long) data used for the visit table.
  - @bryan2018versioncontrol — Git for statistical work, written for beginners.
  - @quarto-books and @rcore2026 — the publishing system and the R software used.
